paragraphs.modern: He said that he had met Socrates fresh from the bath and wearing sandals. Since it was unusual to see Socrates in sandals, Aristodemus asked him where he was going, all dressed up like a dandy.
paragraphs.notes: Named Aristodemus and Socrates in the second sentence to break the he/him chain; 'such a beau' rendered 'all dressed up like a dandy' to keep the joke.

paragraphs.modern: I replied, Aristodemus said, 'I'll do whatever you tell me.'
paragraphs.notes: Keeps Jowett's first-person 'I replied' and adds Plato's recurring 'he said' as 'Aristodemus said', so the 'I' cannot be taken for Apollodorus. The same device is used in 1.26.

paragraphs.modern: and we can support this change with the authority of Homer himself, who not only demolishes the proverb but does outright violence to it. For after portraying Agamemnon as the bravest of men, he has Menelaus, who is only a fainthearted warrior, come uninvited to Agamemnon's banquet while Agamemnon is feasting and offering sacrifices. So in Homer it is not the better who comes uninvited to the worse, but the worse to the better.
paragraphs.notes: Lowercase opening kept because the sentence continues from 1.17-1.18. 'Literally outrages' rendered 'does outright violence to it'.

paragraphs.modern: 'But I'll say that it was you who invited me, and then you'll have to come up with the excuse.'
paragraphs.notes: Quotation marks restored; this continues Aristodemus's speech after the verse in 1.21.

paragraphs.modern: he replied, in Homeric style, 'one or the other of them may think up an excuse on the way.'

This was the style of their conversation as they went along. Then Socrates, lost in thought, dropped behind and told Aristodemus, who had stopped to wait for him, to go on ahead. When Aristodemus reached Agathon's house, he found the doors wide open, and a comical thing happened. A servant coming out met him and led him straight into the dining hall, where the guests were reclining on their couches, for the banquet was about to begin. 'Welcome, Aristodemus,' said Agathon as soon as he appeared. 'You're just in time to have supper with us. If you've come about anything else, put it off and join us. I was looking for you yesterday — I meant to invite you, if only I'd been able to find you. But what have you done with Socrates?'
paragraphs.notes: 'On their couches' added so that 'reclining' is picturable (Greek diners lay on couches), which also prepares 1.30 and 1.36.

paragraphs.modern: I turned around, Aristodemus said, but Socrates was nowhere to be seen. So I had to explain that he had been with me only a moment before, and that I had come to the supper at his invitation.
paragraphs.notes: 'Aristodemus said' tag added after the first clause, parallel to 1.14. 'Said' rather than 'told me', so that 'me' in the next sentence can only be Aristodemus.

paragraphs.modern: The servant then helped him wash, and he took his place, reclining at the table. Soon another servant came in and reported that our friend Socrates had withdrawn into the porch of the house next door. 'He's standing there, rooted to the spot,' the servant said, 'and when I call him, he won't move.'
paragraphs.notes: 'Portico' becomes 'porch' here and in 1.33, where Agathon refers back to it.

paragraphs.modern: 'Well, if you think so, I'll leave him alone,' said Agathon. Then, turning to the servants, he added, 'Let's have supper without waiting for him. Serve whatever you like, since there's no one to give you orders — I've never left you to yourselves before. But this time, imagine that you are our hosts, and that I and the company are your guests. Treat us well, and we'll praise you for it.' After this, supper was served, but still there was no Socrates. During the meal Agathon said several times that he wanted to send for him, but Aristodemus objected. At last, when the feast was about half over — for his trance, as usual, did not last long — Socrates came in. Agathon, who was reclining alone at the end of the table, begged him to take the place next to him, 'so that I can touch you,' he said, 'and get the benefit of that wise thought that came to you in the porch and is now yours. For I'm certain you wouldn't have come away until you had found what you were looking for.'
paragraphs.notes: Purpose link restored ('so that I can touch you'), following Jowett's own 'that I may touch you'. The doubled quotation marks are removed and 'the fit' becomes 'his trance'.

paragraphs.modern: 'How I wish,' said Socrates, taking his place as he had been asked, 'that wisdom could flow by touch from the fuller man into the emptier, the way water creeps along a thread of wool from a fuller cup into an emptier one. If that were so, how highly I would value the privilege of reclining at your side! For you would fill me to the brim with a rich and beautiful stream of wisdom, whereas my own is a very poor and questionable sort, no better than a dream. But yours is bright and full of promise. The day before yesterday, in the theater, it shone out in all the splendor of youth before more than thirty thousand Greeks.'
paragraphs.notes: The wool image is made picturable as water creeping along a thread of wool from cup to cup. 'In the theater' is added so that listeners connect this with Agathon's prize (1.5, 1.13). 'Hellenes' is kept as 'Greeks', as in the accepted modern-en; change it back if the reviewer wants Jowett's form of the name.

paragraphs.modern: 'You're mocking me, Socrates,' said Agathon. 'Before long, you and I will have to settle which of us carries off the prize for wisdom, and Dionysus, god of wine and the theater, will be our judge. But for now, you'd better get on with your supper.'
paragraphs.notes: Dionysus is glossed in five words. 'Bears off the palm' becomes 'carries off the prize'.

paragraphs.modern: Socrates took his place on the couch and ate supper with the others. Then they poured out offerings of wine to the gods, sang a hymn to the god, and went through the other customary rites. They were about to start drinking when Pausanias said, 'Now, my friends, how can we drink with the least harm to ourselves? I can tell you that I'm still suffering badly from yesterday's drinking and need time to recover — and I suspect most of you are in the same state, since you were at the party yesterday too. So think it over: how can we make the drinking as easy as possible?'
paragraphs.notes: 'Libations' is rendered as offerings of wine poured for the gods. Jowett's singular 'the god' for the hymn is kept.

paragraphs.modern: 'In that case,' said Eryximachus, 'those of us who cannot hold our wine — myself, Aristodemus, Phaedrus, and others who can never drink much — are fortunate to find that the strong drinkers are not in the mood for drinking. I do not count Socrates: he can drink or abstain equally well, and will not mind whichever we do. Well, since none of the company seems inclined to drink much, I may be forgiven for saying, as a physician, that heavy drinking is a bad practice. I never indulge in it if I can help it, and I certainly do not recommend it to anyone else — least of all to someone who is still feeling the effects of yesterday's excesses.'
paragraphs.notes: 'Weak heads' becomes 'can't hold our wine', and 'carouse' becomes 'excesses', which keeps the doctor's pomposity. Jowett's parenthesis about Socrates becomes its own sentence.

paragraphs.modern: 'I will begin,' he said, 'by borrowing Melanippe's line from a play by Euripides:'
paragraphs.notes: Tells the reader that the next line (1.45, 'Not mine the word') is borrowed. The colon inside the quotation follows the kept 1.15.

paragraphs.modern: 'that I am about to speak, but Phaedrus's. For he often complains to me indignantly, "How strange it is, Eryximachus, that other gods have poems and hymns composed in their honor, while the great and glorious god Love has not a single poet to praise him, out of all the many poets there are. The worthy sophists too — professional teachers such as the excellent Prodicus — have written prose speeches praising the virtues of Heracles and other heroes. And what is even more extraordinary, I once came across a philosophical book in which the usefulness of salt was made the subject of an eloquent speech, and many other things like that have been honored in the same way. Just think: people have taken such an eager interest in things like these, and yet to this day no one has ever dared to sing Love's praises as he deserves! That is how completely this great god has been neglected." Now I think Phaedrus is quite right about this, and so I want to offer him a contribution. Besides, I think that at this moment we who are gathered here could do nothing better than honor the god Love. If you agree with me, there will be no shortage of conversation, because I propose that each of us in turn, going from left to right, should make a speech in honor of Love. Let each of us give the best speech he can; and Phaedrus should begin, because he is sitting first on the left, and because he is the father of the idea.'
paragraphs.notes: Phaedrus's complaint is marked with straight double quotation marks nested inside Eryximachus's single-quoted speech, so it clearly ends before 'Now I think Phaedrus is quite right'. 'Sophists' is glossed as professional teachers, and 'sophists ... have written' fixes Jowett's 'Prodicus ... who have' agreement.

paragraphs.modern: 'No one will vote against you, Eryximachus,' said Socrates. 'How could I oppose your motion, when the only subject I claim to understand is love? Nor, I imagine, will Agathon and Pausanias; and there's certainly no doubt about Aristophanes, the comic poet, whose whole concern is with Dionysus and Aphrodite — that is, with wine and the theater, and with love. Nor will anyone else I see around me disagree. I'm aware that the proposal may seem rather hard on those of us whose turn comes last, but we'll be content if we hear some good speeches first. Let Phaedrus begin the praise of Love, and good luck to him.' All the company agreed, and urged Phaedrus to do as Socrates had said.
paragraphs.notes: Jowett's closing 'him' is identified as Phaedrus, the person Socrates told to begin.

paragraphs.modern: Phaedrus began by declaring that Love is a mighty god, wonderful among gods and men, but especially wonderful in his birth. For he is the eldest of the gods, which is an honor to him; and the proof of his claim to this honor is that there is no record of his parents. No poet or prose writer has ever said that he had any. As the poet Hesiod says:
In other words, after Chaos, these two came into being: Earth and Love. And the philosopher-poet Parmenides sings of Generation, the power that brings things into being, as the maker of Love:
paragraphs.notes: Over 125% of Jowett's length because of the two glosses the fix asks for. Parmenides is called a philosopher-poet. Generation is described as 'the power that brings things into being' and 'the maker of Love', so the 'he' in the kept verse (2.3) clearly means Generation, not Parmenides.

paragraphs.modern: And Acusilaus, an early prose writer on the origins of the gods, agrees with Hesiod. So there are many witnesses who acknowledge that Love is the eldest of the gods. And he is not only the eldest; he is also the source of the greatest benefits to us. For I know of no greater blessing for a young man who is starting out in life than a virtuous lover — an older man who loves and courts him — and no greater blessing for the lover than a beloved youth. For there is a principle that ought to guide men who want to live nobly, and I say that neither family, nor public honors, nor wealth, nor any other motive can instill that principle as well as love can. What do I mean? The sense of honor and dishonor, without which neither states nor individuals ever do any good or great work. And I say that if a lover is caught doing something dishonorable, or letting another man dishonor him because he is too cowardly to resist, he will be more pained to be seen by his beloved than by his father, his companions, or anyone else. The beloved, too, feels the same way about his lover when he is caught in any disgraceful situation. So if only there were some way to form a state or an army made up of lovers and their beloveds, they would be the very best governors of their own city, holding back from everything dishonorable and competing with one another for honor. And fighting side by side, even a mere handful of them would overcome the world.
paragraphs.notes: Acusilaus is glossed as an early prose writer on the origins of the gods. The roles are set out once: the lover is 'an older man who loves and courts him', and the beloved is the youth. In Jowett's list 'honour' is rendered 'public honors', so that it is not confused with the 'sense of honor' that love instills.

paragraphs.modern: For what lover would not rather be seen by the whole of mankind than by his beloved when he was deserting his post or throwing away his weapons? He would be ready to die a thousand deaths rather than endure that. Or who would desert his beloved, or fail him in the hour of danger? At such a time even the worst coward would become an inspired hero, equal to the bravest — Love would inspire him. Homer says that a god breathes courage into the souls of some heroes; Love, by his very nature, gives that same courage to the lover.
paragraphs.notes: 'Arms' is rendered 'weapons' so that it cannot be read as limbs. Jowett's 'the god' becomes 'a god', since Homer's phrase names no particular god here.

paragraphs.modern: Love, and love alone, will make men dare to die for their beloved — and women as well as men. Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, stands as proof of this before all Greece. She was willing to lay down her life for her husband when no one else would, although he had a father and a mother. But her love was so much tenderer than theirs that she made them seem like strangers to their own son, as if they were not his own flesh and blood but related to him in name only. And her deed seemed so noble, to the gods as well as to men, that of the many who have done noble deeds, she is one of the very few to whom the gods, in admiration of what she did, have granted the privilege of coming back alive to earth from the dead. That is how highly the gods honor devotion and virtue in love. But when Orpheus the harper, the son of Oeagrus, went down to Hades for his dead wife, the gods sent him away empty-handed. They showed him only a phantom of the woman he had come for, and would not give her up herself, because he showed no spirit. He was only a harp-player, and did not dare, as Alcestis did, to die for love; instead, he schemed to find a way into Hades while still alive. What is more, the gods later had him put to death at the hands of women, as the punishment for his cowardice.
paragraphs.notes: 'Went down to Hades for his dead wife' is added, as the fix asks; she is not named, because Jowett does not name her. 'Hellas' is given as 'Greece', as in the accepted modern-en.

paragraphs.modern: Very different was the reward Achilles received for his true love toward Patroclus, who was his lover and not his beloved — that is, Patroclus was the older man who loved him, and Achilles the younger man he loved. The idea that Patroclus was the beloved is a foolish mistake made by the tragic poet Aeschylus, for Achilles was surely the more beautiful of the two, and more beautiful than all the other heroes too; and, as Homer tells us, he was still beardless and much younger. The gods do greatly honor the virtue of love; but they admire, value, and reward it even more when the beloved returns the love of his lover, for the lover is more divine, since he is inspired by a god. Now Achilles knew very well, because his mother had told him, that if he held back from killing Hector — the Trojan who had killed Patroclus — he could escape death, return home, and live to a ripe old age. Nevertheless he gave his life to avenge his friend, and dared to die for him — not only to defend him, but even after Patroclus was already dead. That is why the gods honored him even above Alcestis, and sent him to the Islands of the Blessed. These are my reasons for declaring that Love is the eldest, the noblest, and the mightiest of the gods, and the chief author and giver of virtue in life and of happiness after death.
paragraphs.notes: Jowett's parenthesis about Aeschylus becomes ordinary sentences, with nothing left out. The roles are stated plainly. Hector is glossed as Patroclus's killer. 'Inspired by God' becomes 'inspired by a god', and 'Wherefore' becomes 'That is why', so it is plain that the ranking above Alcestis follows from the beloved's greater honor. 'Islands of the Blest' is spelled 'Islands of the Blessed', as in the accepted text.
